items.stem: A task has PV = 100, EV = 80, AC = 90. What is the schedule variance (SV)?

options.rationale: Correct: SV = EV - PV = 80 - 100 = -20, indicating the work is behind schedule.
SV uses EV - PV, not EV - AC; the result is -20, not +10.
-10 would be the cost variance (EV - AC), not the schedule variance.
EV and PV differ, so SV is not zero.

items.explanation: Correct: SV = EV - PV = 80 - 100 = -20, indicating the work is behind schedule.

items.stem: Which earned value method is most appropriate for a long task with no tangible interim deliverables, measured by proportion of time elapsed only as a last resort?

options.rationale: Correct: LOE is used for support-type work without discrete deliverables; its EV tracks the time-phased plan.
0/100 suits short tasks credited only at completion, not ongoing support work.
Units complete needs countable discrete outputs, which this task lacks.
Apportioned effort ties to a discrete base measure, which is not described here.

items.explanation: Correct: LOE is used for support-type work without discrete deliverables; its EV tracks the time-phased plan.

items.stem: Which TWO actions protect the integrity of an EVM performance measurement baseline? (Select TWO)

options.text: Controlling baseline changes through formal change control
options.rationale: Correct: formal change control preserves baseline integrity.

options.text: Preventing retroactive changes to closed reporting periods
options.rationale: Correct: locking prior periods prevents manipulation and preserves integrity.

options.text: Adjusting EV upward to meet targets
options.rationale: Altering EV to hit targets is data manipulation and destroys integrity.
Informal re-baselining bypasses control and corrupts the PMB.

items.explanation: Correct: formal change control preserves baseline integrity.
